title: Another 4 ways in which teachers can help or hinder learning
author: Martin Skelton
summary: Skelton completes his list of nine attributes of good-enough learning-focused teachers, starting from a Twitter exchange where Robert Pondiscio argued the job must be doable by ordinary teachers, not saints and superstars. He agrees and says teachers need to be good at a few things and accept that they are one factor among many. The four new attributes are knowing students and yourself, working positively with parents, modelling what the school hopes students will become, and remaining a learner oneself. The modelling section uses the contrast between Mrs M and Mrs D to show how emotional and social behaviour is learned alongside academic content because learning is always on. He insists this is not soft teaching and shows his own Duolingo Spanish as a way of keeping the learner's struggle fresh. The post ends with a ten-point teacher checklist.
points: Good-enough teaching, not heroic teaching, is the realistic target for a large workforce, a point Skelton takes from Pondiscio and Winnicott's good-enough parent.
Self-knowledge matters because a teacher's own irritations and discomforts shape which pupils get a better or worse deal.
Teachers who accept parents' limitations as a starting point, much as they accept pupils' fragilities, stay constructive rather than blaming.
Mrs M and Mrs D show that teachers' emotional modelling becomes the class culture and affects academic learning as well as social behaviour.
Teachers should keep experiencing good and bad struggle in their own learning so they stay sympathetic without becoming soft.
quotes: Robert Pondiscio replied to Michael Brand and said that ‘The job must be ‘doable’ by the teachers we have. A workforce that large can’t be for saints and superstars only. There aren’t enough of them to go around.
We need to be good at a few things and not brilliant at everything. We certainly don’t need to know everything. We also need to accept that we are just one of the factors that affect learning.

Learning-focused teachers may regret that some of their children and students haven’t learned as well as others but they don’t translate that regret into disappointment and discouragement; they accept it as their starting point from which learning can and will happen. These teachers accept their children and students as they are, academically, socially, emotionally and physically, and work towards enabling them to get better.

I am not suggesting that every teacher needs therapy. But in classrooms where children and students are lucky enough to be able to mostly learn well, then their teachers know that their own foibles and idiosyncrasies have an important influence on that learning. In knowing that, they are able to self-monitor and make the necessary adjustments not only to their plans, equipment or resources but also, over time, to themselves.

For reasons I was never able to fathom, she arrived at school angry and got angrier during the day. She was angry with herself, with her family, with her colleagues and, above all with her class. Where Mrs M helped her students strategise about and overcome their interpersonal problems and squabbles, Mrs D simply exacerbated them.

I have met and worked with some unbelievably fine and dedicated learning-focused teachers in my time but none of them were in any way ‘soft’. They required hard work and focus from their students, the existence of classroom cultures in which everyone could learn, and they demonstrated a refusal to shower compliments on the students in their classes for work which wasn’t enabling their students to be the ‘best they can be.

What matters is that these teachers are continuing to have the same sort of good and bad struggles that their children and students are currently having. These experiences enable these teachers to be more sympathetic (this doesn’t mean soft) towards their children and students than teachers who long ago left their own learning behind.
